subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on enzymes and digestion, then mark my answer against the spec.
promptWeak: Explain enzymes and digestion for GCSE simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Enzymes as biological catalysts and the lock-and-key model
Effect of temperature and pH on enzyme activity and denaturation
Structure and function of the human digestive system
Digestive enzymes: amylase, protease and lipase
Absorption and the adaptations of villi
Food tests for reducing sugar, starch, protein and fat

questions.lo: Enzymes as biological catalysts and the lock-and-key model
questions.q: What is an enzyme?
options: A biological catalyst that speeds up reactions
A fatty acid used to build membranes
A hormone that carries messages in the blood
questions.explain: Enzymes are biological catalysts. They speed up the rate of chemical reactions in living organisms without being used up themselves.

questions.lo: Enzymes as biological catalysts and the lock-and-key model
questions.q: Enzymes are made of which type of molecule?
questions.explain: Enzymes are proteins. Their specific 3D shape, including the active site, comes from the way the protein is folded.

questions.lo: Enzymes as biological catalysts and the lock-and-key model
questions.q: In the lock-and-key model, why can each enzyme only act on one type of substrate?
options: The substrate must be the same colour as the enzyme
Enzymes randomly bind any molecule they touch
The active site has a complementary shape to only that substrate
The substrate is always larger than the enzyme
questions.explain: The active site has a specific shape that is complementary to only one substrate, like a key fitting one lock. Other substrates do not fit, so the enzyme is specific.

questions.lo: Enzymes as biological catalysts and the lock-and-key model
questions.q: What name is given to the region of an enzyme where the substrate binds?
questions.explain: The active site is the part of the enzyme where the substrate binds to form an enzyme-substrate complex.

questions.lo: Effect of temperature and pH on enzyme activity and denaturation
questions.q: As temperature increases from 10 C to the optimum, what happens to the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction?
options: It increases because molecules move faster and collide more often
questions.explain: Up to the optimum, raising the temperature gives molecules more kinetic energy, so enzyme and substrate collide more frequently and the rate increases.

questions.lo: Effect of temperature and pH on enzyme activity and denaturation
questions.q: What happens to an enzyme when it is denatured by a high temperature?
options: It works faster than ever before
The shape of its active site changes so the substrate no longer fits
It multiplies to make more enzyme
questions.explain: High temperatures break the bonds holding the enzyme's shape. The active site changes shape, the substrate no longer fits, and the enzyme is denatured and cannot work.

questions.lo: Effect of temperature and pH on enzyme activity and denaturation
questions.q: Pepsin, a protease in the stomach, has an optimum pH of about 2. In which condition will it work best?
options: It works equally at all pH values
questions.explain: Pepsin works in the acidic stomach, so its optimum pH is around 2 (strongly acidic). Away from this optimum its activity falls and it can denature.

questions.lo: Effect of temperature and pH on enzyme activity and denaturation
questions.q: Which statement about denaturation caused by extreme pH is correct?
options: It permanently changes the shape of the active site
It speeds the enzyme up permanently
It is always reversible when pH returns to normal
questions.explain: Extreme pH (like high temperature) permanently alters the shape of the active site, so the enzyme is denatured and cannot catalyse its reaction.

questions.lo: Structure and function of the human digestive system
questions.q: Where does most absorption of digested food into the blood take place?
questions.explain: Digested soluble molecules are absorbed mainly across the wall of the small intestine (ileum), which is highly adapted for absorption.

questions.lo: Structure and function of the human digestive system
questions.q: What is digestion?
options: The build-up of small molecules into large ones
The movement of blood around the body
The breakdown of large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones
questions.explain: Digestion is the breakdown of large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood.

questions.lo: Structure and function of the human digestive system
questions.q: Which organ produces amylase, protease and lipase and releases them into the small intestine?
questions.explain: The pancreas produces amylase, protease and lipase enzymes and releases them into the small intestine.

questions.lo: Digestive enzymes: amylase, protease and lipase
questions.q: Amylase breaks down starch into which product?
questions.explain: Amylase (a carbohydrase) breaks down starch into simple sugars such as maltose.

questions.lo: Digestive enzymes: amylase, protease and lipase
questions.q: Which enzyme breaks down proteins into amino acids?
questions.explain: Proteases break down proteins into amino acids.

questions.lo: Digestive enzymes: amylase, protease and lipase
questions.q: Lipase breaks down fats (lipids) into which products?
questions.explain: Lipase breaks down fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.lo: The role of bile
questions.q: Where is bile produced?
questions.explain: Bile is produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder before being released into the small intestine.

questions.lo: The role of bile
questions.q: Bile emulsifies fats. What does this mean and why is it useful?
options: It breaks large fat droplets into smaller droplets, increasing surface area for lipase
It chemically digests fat into amino acids
It neutralises all enzymes in the gut
It absorbs fat directly into the blood
questions.explain: Bile emulsifies fats by breaking large fat droplets into many small droplets. This increases the surface area for lipase to act on, speeding up fat digestion. Bile also neutralises stomach acid.

questions.lo: Absorption and the adaptations of villi
questions.q: Which feature of villi increases the surface area for absorption in the small intestine?
options: Their large number of tiny finger-like projections
questions.explain: Villi are tiny finger-like projections that greatly increase the surface area of the small intestine for absorption.

questions.lo: Absorption and the adaptations of villi
questions.q: Villi have a thin (one-cell-thick) wall and a good blood supply. How do these adaptations aid absorption?
options: They prevent any molecules entering the blood
They slow diffusion so food is not lost
They shorten the diffusion distance and maintain a concentration gradient
They make the food more acidic
questions.explain: A thin wall gives a short diffusion distance, and a good blood supply carries absorbed molecules away, maintaining a steep concentration gradient for efficient absorption.

questions.lo: Food tests for reducing sugar, starch, protein and fat
questions.q: A student adds iodine solution to a sample and it turns blue-black. What does this show?
questions.explain: Iodine solution turns from orange-brown to blue-black in the presence of starch.

questions.lo: Food tests for reducing sugar, starch, protein and fat
questions.q: Which test result correctly identifies its food group?
options: Benedict's turns brick-red when heated = protein
questions.explain: Biuret solution turns from blue to purple/lilac with protein. Benedict's turns brick-red with reducing sugar, iodine turns blue-black with starch, and the ethanol emulsion test gives a cloudy white layer with fat.

specSource: CCEA GCSE Biology (2017) specification; Enzymes & Digestion
